sourceDefinition: The first letter of the alphabet [according to the order in which the letters are now commonly disposed; and also according to the original order, which see in art. Abjd ]: called A^alifN . [This name, like most of the other names of Arabic letters, is traceable to the Phœnician language, in which it signifies “an ox;” the ancient Phœnician form of the letter thus called being a rude representation of an ox's head.] It is, of all the letters, that which is most frequent in speech: and some say that, in A=l=m= , in the Kur [ch. ii. &c.], it is a name of God. (TA.) Its name is properly fem., as is also that of every other letter; [and hence its pl. is A^alifaAtN ;] but it may be made masc.: so says Ks: Sb says that all the letters of the alphabet are masc. and fem., like as Al~isaAnN is masc. and fem. (M.) As a letter of the alphabet, it is abbreviated, [or short, and is written A , as it also is generally when occurring in a word, except at the end, when, in certain cases, it is written Y ,] and is pronounced with a pause after it: and it is also prolonged: (S, K, * TA:) [in the latter case, it is written A='N ; and] this is the case when it is made a subst.: and when it is not called a letter, [i. e. when one does not prefix to it the word Harof ,] it is [properly] fem. (S.) Its dim. is A^uyay~apN , meaning an A' written small, or obscure, (S, IB,) according to those who make it fem. and who say, zay~ayatu zaAyFA and *ay~alotu *aAlFA ; but A^uway~apN according to those who say, zaw~ayotu zaAyFA . (IB.) -A2- A^alifN [properly so called] is one of the letters of prolongation and of softness and of augmentation; the letters of augmentation being ten, which are comprised in the saying, Alyawoma tanosaAhu [“to-day thou wilt forget it”]. (S.) There are two species of Alf ; namely, lay~inapN [or soft ], and mutaHar~ikapN [or movent ]; the former of which is [properly] called A^alifN ; and the latter, hamozapN ; (S, TA;) which is a faucial letter, pronounced in the furthest part of the fauces [by a sudden emission of the voice after a total suppression, so that it resembles in sound a feebly-uttered E whence the form of the character ( ' ) whereby it is represented]: but this latter is sometimes tropically called Alf ; and both [as shown above] are of the letters of augmentation. (S in art. Aw , and TA.) There are also two other species of Alf ; namely, A^alifu waSolK [ the alif of conjunction or connexion, or the conjunctive or connexive alif ]; and A^alifu qaToEK [ the alif of disjunction, or the disjunctive alif ]; every one that is permanent in the connexion of words being of the latter species; and that which is not permanent, [i. e. which is not pronounced, unless it is an alif of prolongation,] of the former species; and this is without exception augmentative; [but it is sometimes a substitute for a suppressed radical letter, as in A@bonN , originally banaYN or banawN ;] whereas the alif of disjunction is sometimes augmentative, as in the case of the interrogative alif [to be mentioned below, and in other cases]; and sometimes radical, as in A^axa*a and A^amara : (S, TA:) or, according to Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà and Mohammad Ibn-Yezeed, (T, TA,) the primary A^alifaAt are three; the rest being subordinate to these: namely, A^alifN A^aSoliy~apN [ radical alif ], (T, K, TA,) as in A_ilofN and A^akala (T) and A^axa*a ; (K;) and A^alifN qaToEiyapN [ disjunctive alif ], as in A^aHomadu (T, K) and A^aHomaru (T) and A^aHosana ; (T, K;) and A^alifN waSoliy~apN [ conjunctive or connexive alif ], (T, K,) as in A@sotaxoraAjN (T) and A@sotaxoraja . (T, K.) ― -b2- The A^alif which is one of the letters of prolongation and of softness is called AlA^alifu AlhaAdiy^apu [ the quiescent alif, and AlA^alifu Als~aAkinapu , which signifies the same]: (MF, TA:) it is an aerial letter, (Mughnee, MF, TA,) merely a sound of prolongation after a fet-hah; (T, TA;) and cannot have a vowel, (IB, Mughnee, MF,) wherefore it cannot commence a word: (Mughnee:) when they desire to make it movent, if it is converted from w or Y , they restore it to its original, as in EaSawaAni and raHayaAni ; and if it is not converted from w or Y , they substitute for it hemzeh, as in rasaAy^ilu , in which the hemzeh is a substitute for the A in [the sing.] rasaAlapN . (IB.) IJ holds that the name of this letter is laA , [pronounced lá or lé, without, or with, imáleh, like the similar names of other letters, as baA and tA and vaA &c.,] and that it is the letter which is mentioned [next] before Y in reckoning the letters; the l being prefixed to it because it cannot be pronounced at the beginning of its name, as other letters can, as, for instance, S and j ; and he adds that the teachers [in schools] err in pronouncing its name laAma A@lifo . (Mughnee.) ― -b3- The grammarians have other particular appellations for alifs, which will be here mentioned. (T, TA.) ― -b4- AlA^alifu Almajohuwlapu [ The unknown alif ] is such as that in faAEilN [or faAEala ] and faAEuwlN ; i. e., every A , (T, K,) of those having no original [from which they are converted, not being originally A^ nor w nor Y , but being merely a formative letter, and hence, app., termed “unknown”], (T,) inserted for the purpose of giving fulness of sound to the fet-hah in a verb and in a noun; (T, K;) and this, when it becomes movent, becomes w , as in the case of xaAtamN and xawaAtimu , becoming w in this case because it is movent, and followed by a quiescent A , which A is the A of the pl., and is also mjhwlp . (T.) ― -b5- A^alifaAtu Almad~aAti [ The alifs of prolongations ] are such as those [which are inserted for the same purpose of giving fulness of sound to the fet-hah] in kalokaAlN , for kalokalN , and xaAtaAmN , for xaAtamN , and daAnaAqN , for daAnaqN . (T, K.) In like manner, w is inserted after a dammeh, as in A^anoZuwru ; and Y after a kesreh, as in $iymaAlN . (TA.) An alif of this species is also called A^alifu AlA_i$obaAEi [ The alif added to give fulness of sound to a fet-hah preceding it]: and so is the alif in manaA used in imitation [of a noun in the accus. case; as when one says, raA^ayotu rajulFA (pronounced rajulaA ) “I saw a man,” and the person to whom these words are addressed says, manaA Whom? ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b6- A^alifu AlS~ilapi [ The alif of annexation, or the annexed alif, ] is that which is an annex to the fet-hah of a rhyme, (T, K,) and to that of the fem. pronoun haA : in the former case as in baAnato suEaAdu waA^amosaY HaboluhaA A@noqaTaEaA in which A is made an annex to the fet-hah of the E [of the rhyme]; and in the saying in the Kur [xxxiii. 10], wataZun~uwna biA@ll~`hi AlZ~unuwnaA , in which the A after the last n is an annex to the fet-hah of that n ; and in other instances in the final words of verses of the Kur-án, as qawaAriyra and salosabiylaA [in lxxvi. 15 and 18]: in the other case as in DarabotuhaA and mararotu bihaA . (T.) The difference between it and A^alifu AlwaSoli is, that the latter is in the beginnings of nouns and verbs, and the former is in the endings of nouns [and verbs]. (T, K.) It is also called A^alifu AlA_iTolaAqi [ The alif of unbinding, because the vowel ending a rhyme prevents its being muqay~d , i. e. “bound” by the preceding consonant]: (Mughnee;) and A^alifu AlfaASilapi [ the alif of the final word of a verse of poetry or of a verse of the Kur-án or of a clause of rhyming prose ]. (TA.) [This last appellation must not be confounded with that which here next follows.] ― -b7- AlA^alifu AlfaASilapi [ The separating alif ] is the A which is written after the w of the pl. to make a separation between that w and what follows it, as in $akaruwA (T, K) and kafaruwA , and in the like of yagozuwA and yadoEuwA [and yaroDawoA ]; but when a pronoun is affixed to the verb, this A , being needless, does not remain: (T:) also the A which makes a separation between the n which is a sign of the fem. gender and the heavy [or doubled] n [in the corroborated form of the aor. and imperative], (T, K,) because a triple combination of n is disliked, (T,) as in [ yafoEalonaAn~i and tafoEalonaAn~i and] AifoEalonaAn~i (T, K) and laA tafoEalonaAn~i . (T.) ― -b8- A^alifu Aln~uwni Alxafiyfapi [ The alif of the light, or single, noon in the contracted corroborated form of the aor. and imperative], as in the phrase in the Kur [xcvi. 15], lanasofaEFA biAln~aASiyapi [explained in art. sfE ], (T, K,) and the phrase [in xii. 32], walayakuwnFA mina AlS~aAgiriyna [ And he shall assuredly be of those in a state of vileness, or ignominy ], in both of which instances the pause is made with A [only, without tenween, so that one says lanasofaEaA and layakuwnaA , and this seems to be indicated in Expositions of the Kur-án as the proper pronunciation of these two words in the phrases here cited, the former of which, and the first word of the latter, I find thus written in an excellent copy of the Mughnee, with a fet-hah only instead of tenween, though I find them written in copies of the Kur-án and of the K with tenween, and for this reason only I have written them therewith in the first places above], this A being a substitute for the light n , which is originally the heavy n : and among examples of the same is the saying of El-Aashà, walaAtaHomida Almuvoriyna waA@ll~`ha faA@HomadaA [ And praise not thou the opulent, but God do thou praise ], the poet meaning faA@Homadano , but pausing with an A : (T:) and accord. to 'Ikrimeh Ed-Dabbee, in the saying of Imra-el-Keys, qafaA naboki mino *ikary HabiybK wamanozili [what is meant is, Do thou pause that we may weep by reason of the remembrance of an object of love, and of a place of abode, for] the poet means qifano , but substitutes A for the light n ; (TA;) or, accord. to some, qfA is in this case [a dual] addressed to the poet's two companions. (EM p. 4.) ― -b9- A^alifu AlEiwaDi [ The alif of exchange ] is that which is substituted for the tenween (T, K) of the accus. case when one pauses upon it, (T,) as in raA^ayotu zayodaA (T, K [and so in the copy of the Mughnee mentioned above, but in the copies of the T I find zayodFA ,]) and faEalotu xayoraA and the like. (T.) ― -b10- A^alifu Alt~aEaAyiY [ The alif of inability to express what one desires to say ], (T,) or A^alifa AltagaAbiY [ the alif of feigning negligence or heedlessness ], (K,) [but the former is evidently, in my opinion, the right appellation,] is that which is added when one says A_in~a Eumara , and then, being unable to finish his saying, pauses, saying A_in~a EumaraA , [in the CK EumaraA= ,] prolonging it, desiring to be helped to the speech that should reveal itself to him, (T, K,) and at length saying munoTaliqN , meaning to say, if he were not unable to express it, A_in~a Eumara munoTilaqN [ Verily 'Omar is going away ]. (T.) The A in a case of this kind is [also] said to be lilt~a*ak~uri [ for the purpose of endeavouring to remember ]; and in like manner, w , when one desires to say, yaquwmu zayodN , and, forgetting zyd , prolongs the sound in endeavouring to remember, and says yaquwmuw . (Mughnee in the sections on A and w .) It is also added to a curtailed proper name of a person called to, or hailed, as in yaA EumaA for yaA Eumaru [which is an ex. contrary to rule, as Eumaru is masc. and consists of only three letters]. (T.) ― -b11- A^alifu Aln~udobapi [ The alif of lamentation ], as in waA zayodaAho [ Alas, Zeyd! ], (T, K,) i. e. the A after the d ; (T;) and one may say waA zayodaA , without the h of pausation. (Alfeeyeh of Ibn-Málik, and I 'Ak p. 272.) ― -b12- A^alifu AlA@isotinokaAri [ The alif of disapproval ], (T,) or AlA^alifu liloA_inokaAri [which means the same], (Mughnee,) is similar to that next preceding, as in A^aA^abuw EumaraAh~ [ What! Aboo- 'Omar? ] in reply to one who says, “Aboo-'Omar came;” the h being added in this case after the letter of prolongation like as it is in waA fulaAnaAho said in lamentation. (T.) [The ex. given in the Mughnee is A= EamoraAho , as said in reply to one who says, “I met 'Amr;” and thus I find it written, with A= ; but this is a mistranscription of the interrogative A^a , which see below.] In this case it is only added to give fulness of sound to the vowel; for you say, A^alr~ajuluwho [ What! the man? for A^aA@lr~ajuluwho ,] after one has said “The man stood;” and A^alr~ajulaAho in the accus. case; and A^alr~ajuliyho in the gen. case. (Mughnee in the section on w . [But in my copy of that work, in these instances, the incipient A , which is an A of interrogation, is written A= .]) ― -b13- AlA^alifu Almunoqalibapu Eano yaA='i AlA_iDaAfapi [ The alif that is converted from the affixed pronoun Y ], as in yaA gulaAmaA A^aqobilo [ O my boy, advance thou, ] for yaA gulaAmiY ; (TA in art. Hrz ;) [and yaAEajabaA lizayodK (I 'Ak p. 271) O my wonder at Zeyd! for yA EajabiY lzyd ;] and in yaA A^abataA for yaA A^abatiY , and yaA wayolataA for yaA wayolatiY , and yaAbiA^abaA and yaA biA^abaAho for yaA biA^abiY (T and TA in art. bA^ .) [This is sometimes written Y , but preceded by a fet-hah.] ― -b14- AlA^alifu AlmuHaw~alapu [ The transmuted alif, in some copies of the K A^alifu AlmuHaw~alapi , which, as MF observes, is put for the former,] is every A that is originally w or Y (T, K) movent, (T,) as in qaAla [originally qawala ], and baAEa [originally bayaEa ], (T, K,) and gazaA [originally gazawa ], and qaDaY [originally qaDaY ], and the like of these. (T.) ― -b15- A^alifu Altavoniyapi [ The alif of the dual, or rather, of dualization ], (T, K,) in verbs, (TA,) as in yajolisaAni and ya*ohabaAni , (T, K,) and in nouns, (T,) as in Alz~ayodaAni (T, K) and AlEamoraAni ; (T;) [i. e.] the A which in verbs is a dual pronoun, as in faEalaA and yafuEalaAni , and in nouns a sign of the dual and an indication of the nom. case, as in rajulaAni . (S.) ― -b16- It is also indicative of the accus. case, as in raA^ayotu faAhu [ I saw his mouth ]. (S.) ― -b17- A^alifu AljamoEi [ The alif of the plural, or of pluralization ], as in masaAjidu and jibaAlN (T, K) and furosaAnN and fawaAEilu . (T.) ― -b18- A^alifu Alt~aA^oniyvi [ The alif denoting the fem. gender ], as in HubolaY (Mughnee, K) and sakoraY [in which it is termed maqoSuwrap shortened ], and the meddeh in HamoraA='u (K) and bayoDaA='u and nufasaA='u [in which it is termed mamoduwdap lengthened ]. (TA.) ― -b19- A^alifu AlA_iloHaAqi [ The alif of adjunction, or quasi-coordination; that which renders a word an adjunct to a particular class, i. e. quasi-coordinate to another word, of which the radical letters are more in number than those of the former word, (see the sentence next following,)], (Mughnee, TA,) as in A^aroTFA (Mughnee) [or A^aroTFY ; and the meddeh in EilobaA='N &c.]. ― -b20- A^alifu Altakoviyri [ The alif of multiplication, i. e. that merely augments the number of the letters of a word without making it either fem. or quasi-coordinate to another, unaugmented, word ], as in qabaEovaraY (Mughnee, TA) [correctly qabaEovarFY ], in which the A [here written Y ] is not to denote the fem. gender, (S and K in art. qbEvr ,) because its fem. is qabaEovaraApN , as Mbr. says; (S and TA in that art.;) nor to render it quasi-coordinate to another word, (K and TA in that art.,) as is said in the Lubáb, because there is no noun of six radical letters to which it can be made to be so; but accord. to Ibn-Málik, a word is sometimes made quasi-coordinate to one comprising augmentative letters, as AiqoEanosasa is to AiHoranojama . (TA in that art.) -A3- A^alifaAtu AlwaSoli [ The alifs of conjunction or connexion, or the conjunctive or connexive alifs ], (T, K,) which are in the beginnings of nouns, (T,) [as well as in certain well-known cases in verbs,] occur in A@bonN (T, K) and A@bonumN (K) and A@bonapN and A@vonaAni and A@vonataAni and A@moruw^N and A@moraA^apN and A@somN and A@sotN , (T, K,) which have a kesreh to the A when they commence a sentence, [or occur alone, i. e., when immediately preceded by a quiescence,] but it is elided when they are connected with a preceding word, (T,) [by which term “word” is included a particle consisting of a single letter with its vowel,] and A@yomunN and A@yomu [and variations thereof, which have either a fet-hah or a kesreh to the A when they commence a sentence, or occur alone], (K,) and in the article A@lo , the A of which has a fet-hah when it commences a sentence. (T.) -A4- A^alifu AlqaToEi [ The alif of disjunction, or the disjunctive alif, ] is in the beginnings of sing. nouns and of pl. nouns: it may be known by its permanence in the dim., and by its not being a radical letter: thus it occurs in A^aHosanu , of which the dim. is A^uHayosinu : (I Amb, T:) in pls. it occurs in A^alowaAnN and A^azowaAjN (I Amb, T, K) and A^alosinapN [&c.]: (I Amb, T:) [it also occurs in verbs of the measure A^afoEala , as A^akorama ; in which cases it is sometimes lils~alobi , i. e. privative, (like the Greek alpha,) as in A^aqosaTa “he did away with injustice,” which is termed qusuwTN and qasoTN , inf. ns. of qasaTa :] it is distinguished from the radical A , as shown above: (I Amb, T:) or it is sometimes augmentative, as the interrogative A^a [to be mentioned below]; and sometimes radical, as in A^axa*a and A^amara ; and is thus distinguished from the conjunctive A , which is never other than augmentative. (S.) ― -b2- A^alifu Alt~afoDiyli wa Alt~aqoSiyri [ The alif denoting excess and deficiency, i. e., denoting the comparative and superlative degrees ], as in fulaAnN A^akoramu minoka [ Such a one is more generous, or noble, than thou ], (T, K, *) and A^aloA^amu minoka [ more ungenerous, or ignoble, than thou ], (T,) and A^ajohalu Aln~aAsi [ the most ignorant of men ]. (T, K. *) ― -b3- A^alifu AlEibaArapi [ The alif of signification ], (T, K,) as though, (T,) or because, (TA,) significant of the speaker, (T, TA,) also called AlEaAmilapi [ the operative ], as in A^anaA A^asotagofiru A@ll~`ha [ I beg forgiveness of God ], (T, K,) and A^anaA A^afoEalu ka*aA [ I do thus ]. (T.) ― -b4- A^alifu AlA@isotifohaAmi [ The alif of interrogation, or the interrogative alif ], (T, S, Msb in art. hmz , Mughnee,) as in A^azayodN qaAy^imN [ Is Zeyd standing? ], (Mughnee,) and A^azayodN Einodaka A^amo EamorNw [ Is Zeyd with thee, or at thine abode, or 'Amr? ], (S,) and A^aqaAma zayodN [ Did Zeyd stand? ], said when the asker is in ignorance, and to which the answer is laA or naEamo ; (Msb;) and in a negative phrase, as A^alamo na$oraHo [ Did we not dilate, or enlarge? in the Kur xciv. 1]. (Mughnee.) When this is followed by another hemzeh, an A is interposed between the two hemzehs, [so that you say A^aAA^anota , also written A=A^anota ,] as in the saying of Dhu-r-Rummeh, A^ayaA Zaboyapa AlwaEosaA='a bayona jalaAjilK wabayona Aln~aqaA A^aAA^anoti A^amo A^um~u saAlimi [ O thou doe-gazelle of El-Waasà between Jelájil and the oblong gibbous hill of sand, is it thou, or Umm-Sálim? ]; (T, S;) but some do not this. (T.) [It is often conjoined with A_in~a , as in the Kur xii. 90, A^ay^in~aka laA^anota yuwsufu Art thou indeed Joseph? ] It is sometimes used to make a person acknowledge, or confess, a thing, (T, Msb in art. hmz , Mughnee,) and to establish it, (Msb,) as in the phrase in the Kur [v. 116], A^aA^anota qulota liln~aAsi or A=A^anota [ Didst thou say to men? ], (T,) and A^alamo na$oraHo [explained above], (Msb in art. hmz ,] and in A^aDarabota zayodFA or A^aA^anota Darabota [ Didst thou beat Zeyd? ], and A^azayodFA Darabota [ Zeyd didst thou beat? ]. (Mughnee.) And for reproving, (T, Mughnee,) as in the phrase in the Kur [xxxvii. 153], A^SoTafaY A@lobanaAti EalaY A@lobaniyna [ Hath He chosen daughters in preference to sons? ], (T,) [but see the next sentence,] and [in the same ch., verse 93,] A^ataEobuduwna maA tanoHituwna [ Do ye worship what ye hew out? ]. (Mughnee.) And to express a nullifying denial, as in [the words of the Kur xvii. 42,] A^afaA^aSofaAkumo rab~akumo biA@lobaniyna waA@t~axa*a mina A@lomalaAy^ikapi A_inaAvFA [ Hath then your Lord preferred to give unto you sons, and gotten for himself, of the angels, daughters? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote irony, as in [the Kur xi. 89,] A^aSalawaAtuka taA^omuruka A^ano natoruka maA yaEobudu A=baAw^unaA [ Do thy prayers enjoin thee that we should leave what our fathers worshipped? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote wonder, as in [the Kur xxv.47,] A^alamo tara A_ilaY rab~ika kayofa mad~a A@lZ~il~a [ Hast thou not considered the work of thy Lord, how He hath extended the shade? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote the deeming a thing slow, or tardy, as in [the Kur lvii., 15,] A^alamo yaA^oni lil~*iyna A=manuwA [ Hath not the time yet come for those who have believed? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote a command, as in [the Kur iii. 19,] A^aA^asolamotumo , meaning A^asolimuwA [ Enter ye into the religion of El-Islám ]. (Mughnee, and so Jel.) And to denote equality, occurring after sawaA='N and maA A^ubaAliY and maA A^adoriY and layota $iEoriY , and the like, as in [the Kur lxiii.6,] sawaA='N Ealayohimo A^asotagofarota lahumo A^amo lamo tasotagofiro lahumo [It will be equal to them whether thou beg forgiveness for them or do not beg forgiveness for them ], and in ,aA A^ubaAliY A^aqumota A^amo qaEadota [ I care not whether thou stand or sit ]: and the general rule is this, that it is the hemzeh advening to a phrase, or proposition, of which the place may be supplied by the inf. n. of its verb; for one may say, sawaA='N Ealayohimu A@lA@isotigofaAru waEadamuhu [ Equal to them will be the begging of forgiveness and the not doing so ], and maA A^abaAliY biqiyaAmika waEadamihi [ I care not for thy standing and thy not doing so ]: (Mughnee.) ― -b5- A^alifu Aln~idaA='i [ The alif of calling, or vocative alif ], (T, S,* Mughnee,* K,) as in A^azayodu , meaning yaA zayodu [ O Zeyd ], (T, K,) and in A^azayodu A^aqobilo [ O Zeyd, advance ], (S,) used in calling him who is near, (S, Mughnee,) to the exclusion of him who is distant, because it is abbreviated. (S.) A= with medd, is a particle used in calling to him who is distant, (Mughnee, K,) as in A=azayodu A^aqobilo [ Ho there, or soho, or holla, Zeyd, advance ]. (TA.) Az says, You say to a man, in calling him, A=fulaAnu and A^afulaAnu and A=yaA fulaAnu (TA) or A^ayaA . (S and K in art. AyA .) ― -b6- A_iA@ll~`hi , for A_iYo waA@ll~`hi : see A_iY . ― -b7- In a dial. of some of the Arabs, hemzeh is used in a case of pausing at the end of a verb, as in their saying to a woman, quwliy^o [ Say thou ], and to two men, quwlaA^o [ Say ye two ], and to a pl. number, quwluw^o [ Say ye ]; but not when the verb is connected with a word following it: and they say also laA^o , with a hemzeh, [for laA ,] in a case of pausation. (T.) But Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà says, All men say that when a hemzeh occurs at the end of a word, [i. e. in a case of pausation,] and has a quiescent letter before it, it is elided in the nom. and gen. case, though retained in the accus. case [because followed by a quiescent A ], except Ks alone, who retains it in all cases: when it occurs in the middle of a word, all agree that it should not be dropped. (T.) AZ [however] says that the people of El-Hijáz, and Hudheyl, and the people of Mekkeh and ElMedeeneh, do not pronounce hemzeh [at all]: and 'Eesà Ibn-’Omar says, Temeem pronounce hemzeh, and the people of El-Hijáz, in cases of necessity, [in poetry,] do so. (T.) ― -b8- Ks cites, [as exhibiting two instances of a rare usage of A^aA , or A= , in a case of pausing, in the place of a suppressed word,] Alxayoru xayoraAni wa A_ino $ar~N faA^aA daEaA fulaAnN rab~ahu faA^asomaEaA walaA A^uriydu Al$~ar~a A_il~aA A^ano taA^aA [written without the syll. signs in the MS. from which I transcribe this citation, but the reading seems to be plain, and the meaning, Such a one supplicated his Lord, and made his words to be heard, saying, Good is double good; and if evil be my lot, then evil; but I desire not evil unless Thou will that it should befall me]: and he says, he means, A_il~aA A^ano ta$aA='a ; this being of the dial. of Benoo-Saad, except that it is [with them] taA , with a soft A [only]: also, in replying to a person who says, “Wilt thou not come?” one says, faA^o , meaning faA@*ohabo [ Then go thou with us ]: and in like manner, by fA^A , in the saying above, is meant fa$~ar~N . (TA.) -A5- Hemzeh also sometimes occurs as a verb; A_ih , i. e.! with the A_i of pausation added, being the imperative of waA^aY as syn. with waEada . (Mughnee.) -A6- [As a numeral, 1 denotes One. ]

rawSourceText: The first letter of the alphabet [according to the order in which the letters are now commonly disposed; and also according to the original order, which see in art. Abjd ]: called A^alifN . [This name, like most of the other names of Arabic letters, is traceable to the Phœnician language, in which it signifies “an ox;” the ancient Phœnician form of the letter thus called being a rude representation of an ox's head.] It is, of all the letters, that which is most frequent in speech: and some say that, in A=l=m= , in the Kur [ch. ii. &c.], it is a name of God. (TA.) Its name is properly fem., as is also that of every other letter; [and hence its pl. is A^alifaAtN ;] but it may be made masc.: so says Ks: Sb says that all the letters of the alphabet are masc. and fem., like as Al~isaAnN is masc. and fem. (M.) As a letter of the alphabet, it is abbreviated, [or short, and is written A , as it also is generally when occurring in a word, except at the end, when, in certain cases, it is written Y ,] and is pronounced with a pause after it: and it is also prolonged: (S, K, * TA:) [in the latter case, it is written A='N ; and] this is the case when it is made a subst.: and when it is not called a letter, [i. e. when one does not prefix to it the word Harof ,] it is [properly] fem. (S.) Its dim. is A^uyay~apN , meaning an A' written small, or obscure, (S, IB,) according to those who make it fem. and who say, zay~ayatu zaAyFA and *ay~alotu *aAlFA ; but A^uway~apN according to those who say, zaw~ayotu zaAyFA . (IB.) -A2- A^alifN [properly so called] is one of the letters of prolongation and of softness and of augmentation; the letters of augmentation being ten, which are comprised in the saying, Alyawoma tanosaAhu [“to-day thou wilt forget it”]. (S.) There are two species of Alf ; namely, lay~inapN [or soft ], and mutaHar~ikapN [or movent ]; the former of which is [properly] called A^alifN ; and the latter, hamozapN ; (S, TA;) which is a faucial letter, pronounced in the furthest part of the fauces [by a sudden emission of the voice after a total suppression, so that it resembles in sound a feebly-uttered E whence the form of the character ( ' ) whereby it is represented]: but this latter is sometimes tropically called Alf ; and both [as shown above] are of the letters of augmentation. (S in art. Aw , and TA.) There are also two other species of Alf ; namely, A^alifu waSolK [ the alif of conjunction or connexion, or the conjunctive or connexive alif ]; and A^alifu qaToEK [ the alif of disjunction, or the disjunctive alif ]; every one that is permanent in the connexion of words being of the latter species; and that which is not permanent, [i. e. which is not pronounced, unless it is an alif of prolongation,] of the former species; and this is without exception augmentative; [but it is sometimes a substitute for a suppressed radical letter, as in A@bonN , originally banaYN or banawN ;] whereas the alif of disjunction is sometimes augmentative, as in the case of the interrogative alif [to be mentioned below, and in other cases]; and sometimes radical, as in A^axa*a and A^amara : (S, TA:) or, according to Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà and Mohammad Ibn-Yezeed, (T, TA,) the primary A^alifaAt are three; the rest being subordinate to these: namely, A^alifN A^aSoliy~apN [ radical alif ], (T, K, TA,) as in A_ilofN and A^akala (T) and A^axa*a ; (K;) and A^alifN qaToEiyapN [ disjunctive alif ], as in A^aHomadu (T, K) and A^aHomaru (T) and A^aHosana ; (T, K;) and A^alifN waSoliy~apN [ conjunctive or connexive alif ], (T, K,) as in A@sotaxoraAjN (T) and A@sotaxoraja . (T, K.) ― -b2- The A^alif which is one of the letters of prolongation and of softness is called AlA^alifu AlhaAdiy^apu [ the quiescent alif, and AlA^alifu Als~aAkinapu , which signifies the same]: (MF, TA:) it is an aerial letter, (Mughnee, MF, TA,) merely a sound of prolongation after a fet-hah; (T, TA;) and cannot have a vowel, (IB, Mughnee, MF,) wherefore it cannot commence a word: (Mughnee:) when they desire to make it movent, if it is converted from w or Y , they restore it to its original, as in EaSawaAni and raHayaAni ; and if it is not converted from w or Y , they substitute for it hemzeh, as in rasaAy^ilu , in which the hemzeh is a substitute for the A in [the sing.] rasaAlapN . (IB.) IJ holds that the name of this letter is laA , [pronounced lá or lé, without, or with, imáleh, like the similar names of other letters, as baA and tA and vaA &c.,] and that it is the letter which is mentioned [next] before Y in reckoning the letters; the l being prefixed to it because it cannot be pronounced at the beginning of its name, as other letters can, as, for instance, S and j ; and he adds that the teachers [in schools] err in pronouncing its name laAma A@lifo . (Mughnee.) ― -b3- The grammarians have other particular appellations for alifs, which will be here mentioned. (T, TA.) ― -b4- AlA^alifu Almajohuwlapu [ The unknown alif ] is such as that in faAEilN [or faAEala ] and faAEuwlN ; i. e., every A , (T, K,) of those having no original [from which they are converted, not being originally A^ nor w nor Y , but being merely a formative letter, and hence, app., termed “unknown”], (T,) inserted for the purpose of giving fulness of sound to the fet-hah in a verb and in a noun; (T, K;) and this, when it becomes movent, becomes w , as in the case of xaAtamN and xawaAtimu , becoming w in this case because it is movent, and followed by a quiescent A , which A is the A of the pl., and is also mjhwlp . (T.) ― -b5- A^alifaAtu Almad~aAti [ The alifs of prolongations ] are such as those [which are inserted for the same purpose of giving fulness of sound to the fet-hah] in kalokaAlN , for kalokalN , and xaAtaAmN , for xaAtamN , and daAnaAqN , for daAnaqN . (T, K.) In like manner, w is inserted after a dammeh, as in A^anoZuwru ; and Y after a kesreh, as in $iymaAlN . (TA.) An alif of this species is also called A^alifu AlA_i$obaAEi [ The alif added to give fulness of sound to a fet-hah preceding it]: and so is the alif in manaA used in imitation [of a noun in the accus. case; as when one says, raA^ayotu rajulFA (pronounced rajulaA ) “I saw a man,” and the person to whom these words are addressed says, manaA Whom? ]. (Mughnee.) ― -b6- A^alifu AlS~ilapi [ The alif of annexation, or the annexed alif, ] is that which is an annex to the fet-hah of a rhyme, (T, K,) and to that of the fem. pronoun haA : in the former case as in baAnato suEaAdu waA^amosaY HaboluhaA A@noqaTaEaA in which A is made an annex to the fet-hah of the E [of the rhyme]; and in the saying in the Kur [xxxiii. 10], wataZun~uwna biA@ll~`hi AlZ~unuwnaA , in which the A after the last n is an annex to the fet-hah of that n ; and in other instances in the final words of verses of the Kur-án, as qawaAriyra and salosabiylaA [in lxxvi. 15 and 18]: in the other case as in DarabotuhaA and mararotu bihaA . (T.) The difference between it and A^alifu AlwaSoli is, that the latter is in the beginnings of nouns and verbs, and the former is in the endings of nouns [and verbs]. (T, K.) It is also called A^alifu AlA_iTolaAqi [ The alif of unbinding, because the vowel ending a rhyme prevents its being muqay~d , i. e. “bound” by the preceding consonant]: (Mughnee;) and A^alifu AlfaASilapi [ the alif of the final word of a verse of poetry or of a verse of the Kur-án or of a clause of rhyming prose ]. (TA.) [This last appellation must not be confounded with that which here next follows.] ― -b7- AlA^alifu AlfaASilapi [ The separating alif ] is the A which is written after the w of the pl. to make a separation between that w and what follows it, as in $akaruwA (T, K) and kafaruwA , and in the like of yagozuwA and yadoEuwA [and yaroDawoA ]; but when a pronoun is affixed to the verb, this A , being needless, does not remain: (T:) also the A which makes a separation between the n which is a sign of the fem. gender and the heavy [or doubled] n [in the corroborated form of the aor. and imperative], (T, K,) because a triple combination of n is disliked, (T,) as in [ yafoEalonaAn~i and tafoEalonaAn~i and] AifoEalonaAn~i (T, K) and laA tafoEalonaAn~i . (T.) ― -b8- A^alifu Aln~uwni Alxafiyfapi [ The alif of the light, or single, noon in the contracted corroborated form of the aor. and imperative], as in the phrase in the Kur [xcvi. 15], lanasofaEFA biAln~aASiyapi [explained in art. sfE ], (T, K,) and the phrase [in xii. 32], walayakuwnFA mina AlS~aAgiriyna [ And he shall assuredly be of those in a state of vileness, or ignominy ], in both of which instances the pause is made with A [only, without tenween, so that one says lanasofaEaA and layakuwnaA , and this seems to be indicated in Expositions of the Kur-án as the proper pronunciation of these two words in the phrases here cited, the former of which, and the first word of the latter, I find thus written in an excellent copy of the Mughnee, with a fet-hah only instead of tenween, though I find them written in copies of the Kur-án and of the K with tenween, and for this reason only I have written them therewith in the first places above], this A being a substitute for the light n , which is originally the heavy n : and among examples of the same is the saying of El-Aashà, walaAtaHomida Almuvoriyna waA@ll~`ha faA@HomadaA [ And praise not thou the opulent, but God do thou praise ], the poet meaning faA@Homadano , but pausing with an A : (T:) and accord. to 'Ikrimeh Ed-Dabbee, in the saying of Imra-el-Keys, qafaA naboki mino *ikary HabiybK wamanozili [what is meant is, Do thou pause that we may weep by reason of the remembrance of an object of love, and of a place of abode, for] the poet means qifano , but substitutes A for the light n ; (TA;) or, accord. to some, qfA is in this case [a dual] addressed to the poet's two companions. (EM p. 4.) ― -b9- A^alifu AlEiwaDi [ The alif of exchange ] is that which is substituted for the tenween (T, K) of the accus. case when one pauses upon it, (T,) as in raA^ayotu zayodaA (T, K [and so in the copy of the Mughnee mentioned above, but in the copies of the T I find zayodFA ,]) and faEalotu xayoraA and the like. (T.) ― -b10- A^alifu Alt~aEaAyiY [ The alif of inability to express what one desires to say ], (T,) or A^alifa AltagaAbiY [ the alif of feigning negligence or heedlessness ], (K,) [but the former is evidently, in my opinion, the right appellation,] is that which is added when one says A_in~a Eumara , and then, being unable to finish his saying, pauses, saying A_in~a EumaraA , [in the CK EumaraA= ,] prolonging it, desiring to be helped to the speech that should reveal itself to him, (T, K,) and at length saying munoTaliqN , meaning to say, if he were not unable to express it, A_in~a Eumara munoTilaqN [ Verily 'Omar is going away ]. (T.) The A in a case of this kind is [also] said to be lilt~a*ak~uri [ for the purpose of endeavouring to remember ]; and in like manner, w , when one desires to say, yaquwmu zayodN , and, forgetting zyd , prolongs the sound in endeavouring to remember, and says yaquwmuw . (Mughnee in the sections on A and w .) It is also added to a curtailed proper name of a person called to, or hailed, as in yaA EumaA for yaA Eumaru [which is an ex. contrary to rule, as Eumaru is masc. and consists of only three letters]. (T.) ― -b11- A^alifu Aln~udobapi [ The alif of lamentation ], as in waA zayodaAho [ Alas, Zeyd! ], (T, K,) i. e. the A after the d ; (T;) and one may say waA zayodaA , without the h of pausation. (Alfeeyeh of Ibn-Málik, and I 'Ak p. 272.) ― -b12- A^alifu AlA@isotinokaAri [ The alif of disapproval ], (T,) or AlA^alifu liloA_inokaAri [which means the same], (Mughnee,) is similar to that next preceding, as in A^aA^abuw EumaraAh~ [ What! Aboo- 'Omar? ] in reply to one who says, “Aboo-'Omar came;” the h being added in this case after the letter of prolongation like as it is in waA fulaAnaAho said in lamentation. (T.) [The ex. given in the Mughnee is A= EamoraAho , as said in reply to one who says, “I met 'Amr;” and thus I find it written, with A= ; but this is a mistranscription of the interrogative A^a , which see below.] In this case it is only added to give fulness of sound to the vowel; for you say, A^alr~ajuluwho [ What! the man? for A^aA@lr~ajuluwho ,] after one has said “The man stood;” and A^alr~ajulaAho in the accus. case; and A^alr~ajuliyho in the gen. case. (Mughnee in the section on w . [But in my copy of that work, in these instances, the incipient A , which is an A of interrogation, is written A= .]) ― -b13- AlA^alifu Almunoqalibapu Eano yaA='i AlA_iDaAfapi [ The alif that is converted from the affixed pronoun Y ], as in yaA gulaAmaA A^aqobilo [ O my boy, advance thou, ] for yaA gulaAmiY ; (TA in art. Hrz ;) [and yaAEajabaA lizayodK (I 'Ak p. 271) O my wonder at Zeyd! for yA EajabiY lzyd ;] and in yaA A^abataA for yaA A^abatiY , and yaA wayolataA for yaA wayolatiY , and yaAbiA^abaA and yaA biA^abaAho for yaA biA^abiY (T and TA in art. bA^ .) [This is sometimes written Y , but preceded by a fet-hah.] ― -b14- AlA^alifu AlmuHaw~alapu [ The transmuted alif, in some copies of the K A^alifu AlmuHaw~alapi , which, as MF observes, is put for the former,] is every A that is originally w or Y (T, K) movent, (T,) as in qaAla [originally qawala ], and baAEa [originally bayaEa ], (T, K,) and gazaA [originally gazawa ], and qaDaY [originally qaDaY ], and the like of these. (T.) ― -b15- A^alifu Altavoniyapi [ The alif of the dual, or rather, of dualization ], (T, K,) in verbs, (TA,) as in yajolisaAni and ya*ohabaAni , (T, K,) and in nouns, (T,) as in Alz~ayodaAni (T, K) and AlEamoraAni ; (T;) [i. e.] the A which in verbs is a dual pronoun, as in faEalaA and yafuEalaAni , and in nouns a sign of the dual and an indication of the nom. case, as in rajulaAni . (S.) ― -b16- It is also indicative of the accus. case, as in raA^ayotu faAhu [ I saw his mouth ]. (S.) ― -b17- A^alifu AljamoEi [ The alif of the plural, or of pluralization ], as in masaAjidu and jibaAlN (T, K) and furosaAnN and fawaAEilu . (T.) ― -b18- A^alifu Alt~aA^oniyvi [ The alif denoting the fem. gender ], as in HubolaY (Mughnee, K) and sakoraY [in which it is termed maqoSuwrap shortened ], and the meddeh in HamoraA='u (K) and bayoDaA='u and nufasaA='u [in which it is termed mamoduwdap lengthened ]. (TA.) ― -b19- A^alifu AlA_iloHaAqi [ The alif of adjunction, or quasi-coordination; that which renders a word an adjunct to a particular class, i. e. quasi-coordinate to another word, of which the radical letters are more in number than those of the former word, (see the sentence next following,)], (Mughnee, TA,) as in A^aroTFA (Mughnee) [or A^aroTFY ; and the meddeh in EilobaA='N &c.]. ― -b20- A^alifu Altakoviyri [ The alif of multiplication, i. e. that merely augments the number of the letters of a word without making it either fem. or quasi-coordinate to another, unaugmented, word ], as in qabaEovaraY (Mughnee, TA) [correctly qabaEovarFY ], in which the A [here written Y ] is not to denote the fem. gender, (S and K in art. qbEvr ,) because its fem. is qabaEovaraApN , as Mbr. says; (S and TA in that art.;) nor to render it quasi-coordinate to another word, (K and TA in that art.,) as is said in the Lubáb, because there is no noun of six radical letters to which it can be made to be so; but accord. to Ibn-Málik, a word is sometimes made quasi-coordinate to one comprising augmentative letters, as AiqoEanosasa is to AiHoranojama . (TA in that art.) -A3- A^alifaAtu AlwaSoli [ The alifs of conjunction or connexion, or the conjunctive or connexive alifs ], (T, K,) which are in the beginnings of nouns, (T,) [as well as in certain well-known cases in verbs,] occur in A@bonN (T, K) and A@bonumN (K) and A@bonapN and A@vonaAni and A@vonataAni and A@moruw^N and A@moraA^apN and A@somN and A@sotN , (T, K,) which have a kesreh to the A when they commence a sentence, [or occur alone, i. e., when immediately preceded by a quiescence,] but it is elided when they are connected with a preceding word, (T,) [by which term “word” is included a particle consisting of a single letter with its vowel,] and A@yomunN and A@yomu [and variations thereof, which have either a fet-hah or a kesreh to the A when they commence a sentence, or occur alone], (K,) and in the article A@lo , the A of which has a fet-hah when it commences a sentence. (T.) -A4- A^alifu AlqaToEi [ The alif of disjunction, or the disjunctive alif, ] is in the beginnings of sing. nouns and of pl. nouns: it may be known by its permanence in the dim., and by its not being a radical letter: thus it occurs in A^aHosanu , of which the dim. is A^uHayosinu : (I Amb, T:) in pls. it occurs in A^alowaAnN and A^azowaAjN (I Amb, T, K) and A^alosinapN [&c.]: (I Amb, T:) [it also occurs in verbs of the measure A^afoEala , as A^akorama ; in which cases it is sometimes lils~alobi , i. e. privative, (like the Greek alpha,) as in A^aqosaTa “he did away with injustice,” which is termed qusuwTN and qasoTN , inf. ns. of qasaTa :] it is distinguished from the radical A , as shown above: (I Amb, T:) or it is sometimes augmentative, as the interrogative A^a [to be mentioned below]; and sometimes radical, as in A^axa*a and A^amara ; and is thus distinguished from the conjunctive A , which is never other than augmentative. (S.) ― -b2- A^alifu Alt~afoDiyli wa Alt~aqoSiyri [ The alif denoting excess and deficiency, i. e., denoting the comparative and superlative degrees ], as in fulaAnN A^akoramu minoka [ Such a one is more generous, or noble, than thou ], (T, K, *) and A^aloA^amu minoka [ more ungenerous, or ignoble, than thou ], (T,) and A^ajohalu Aln~aAsi [ the most ignorant of men ]. (T, K. *) ― -b3- A^alifu AlEibaArapi [ The alif of signification ], (T, K,) as though, (T,) or because, (TA,) significant of the speaker, (T, TA,) also called AlEaAmilapi [ the operative ], as in A^anaA A^asotagofiru A@ll~`ha [ I beg forgiveness of God ], (T, K,) and A^anaA A^afoEalu ka*aA [ I do thus ]. (T.) ― -b4- A^alifu AlA@isotifohaAmi [ The alif of interrogation, or the interrogative alif ], (T, S, Msb in art. hmz , Mughnee,) as in A^azayodN qaAy^imN [ Is Zeyd standing? ], (Mughnee,) and A^azayodN Einodaka A^amo EamorNw [ Is Zeyd with thee, or at thine abode, or 'Amr? ], (S,) and A^aqaAma zayodN [ Did Zeyd stand? ], said when the asker is in ignorance, and to which the answer is laA or naEamo ; (Msb;) and in a negative phrase, as A^alamo na$oraHo [ Did we not dilate, or enlarge? in the Kur xciv. 1]. (Mughnee.) When this is followed by another hemzeh, an A is interposed between the two hemzehs, [so that you say A^aAA^anota , also written A=A^anota ,] as in the saying of Dhu-r-Rummeh, A^ayaA Zaboyapa AlwaEosaA='a bayona jalaAjilK wabayona Aln~aqaA A^aAA^anoti A^amo A^um~u saAlimi [ O thou doe-gazelle of El-Waasà between Jelájil and the oblong gibbous hill of sand, is it thou, or Umm-Sálim? ]; (T, S;) but some do not this. (T.) [It is often conjoined with A_in~a , as in the Kur xii. 90, A^ay^in~aka laA^anota yuwsufu Art thou indeed Joseph? ] It is sometimes used to make a person acknowledge, or confess, a thing, (T, Msb in art. hmz , Mughnee,) and to establish it, (Msb,) as in the phrase in the Kur [v. 116], A^aA^anota qulota liln~aAsi or A=A^anota [ Didst thou say to men? ], (T,) and A^alamo na$oraHo [explained above], (Msb in art. hmz ,] and in A^aDarabota zayodFA or A^aA^anota Darabota [ Didst thou beat Zeyd? ], and A^azayodFA Darabota [ Zeyd didst thou beat? ]. (Mughnee.) And for reproving, (T, Mughnee,) as in the phrase in the Kur [xxxvii. 153], A^SoTafaY A@lobanaAti EalaY A@lobaniyna [ Hath He chosen daughters in preference to sons? ], (T,) [but see the next sentence,] and [in the same ch., verse 93,] A^ataEobuduwna maA tanoHituwna [ Do ye worship what ye hew out? ]. (Mughnee.) And to express a nullifying denial, as in [the words of the Kur xvii. 42,] A^afaA^aSofaAkumo rab~akumo biA@lobaniyna waA@t~axa*a mina A@lomalaAy^ikapi A_inaAvFA [ Hath then your Lord preferred to give unto you sons, and gotten for himself, of the angels, daughters? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote irony, as in [the Kur xi. 89,] A^aSalawaAtuka taA^omuruka A^ano natoruka maA yaEobudu A=baAw^unaA [ Do thy prayers enjoin thee that we should leave what our fathers worshipped? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote wonder, as in [the Kur xxv.47,] A^alamo tara A_ilaY rab~ika kayofa mad~a A@lZ~il~a [ Hast thou not considered the work of thy Lord, how He hath extended the shade? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote the deeming a thing slow, or tardy, as in [the Kur lvii., 15,] A^alamo yaA^oni lil~*iyna A=manuwA [ Hath not the time yet come for those who have believed? ]. (Mughnee.) And to denote a command, as in [the Kur iii. 19,] A^aA^asolamotumo , meaning A^asolimuwA [ Enter ye into the religion of El-Islám ]. (Mughnee, and so Jel.) And to denote equality, occurring after sawaA='N and maA A^ubaAliY and maA A^adoriY and layota $iEoriY , and the like, as in [the Kur lxiii.6,] sawaA='N Ealayohimo A^asotagofarota lahumo A^amo lamo tasotagofiro lahumo [It will be equal to them whether thou beg forgiveness for them or do not beg forgiveness for them ], and in ,aA A^ubaAliY A^aqumota A^amo qaEadota [ I care not whether thou stand or sit ]: and the general rule is this, that it is the hemzeh advening to a phrase, or proposition, of which the place may be supplied by the inf. n. of its verb; for one may say, sawaA='N Ealayohimu A@lA@isotigofaAru waEadamuhu [ Equal to them will be the begging of forgiveness and the not doing so ], and maA A^abaAliY biqiyaAmika waEadamihi [ I care not for thy standing and thy not doing so ]: (Mughnee.) ― -b5- A^alifu Aln~idaA='i [ The alif of calling, or vocative alif ], (T, S,* Mughnee,* K,) as in A^azayodu , meaning yaA zayodu [ O Zeyd ], (T, K,) and in A^azayodu A^aqobilo [ O Zeyd, advance ], (S,) used in calling him who is near, (S, Mughnee,) to the exclusion of him who is distant, because it is abbreviated. AyA .) ― -b6- A_iA@ll~`hi , for A_iYo waA@ll~`hi : see A_iY . ― -b7- In a dial. of some of the Arabs, hemzeh is used in a case of pausing at the end of a verb, as in their saying to a woman, quwliy^o [ Say thou ], and to two men, quwlaA^o [ Say ye two ], and to a pl. number, quwluw^o [ Say ye ]; but not when the verb is connected with a word following it: and they say also laA^o , with a hemzeh, [for laA ,] in a case of pausation. sourceDefinition: and A_ivofiy~apN [the former of which is the more common, and this only I find in copies of the T,] The stone [ which is one of the three ] whereon the cooking-pot is placed: (A'Obeyd, M, K:) it is, with the Arabs, a stone like the head of a man: (T:) the pl. is A^avaAfiy~u and A^avaAfK ; (T, S, [in which latter it is written differently in different copies, with the article prefixed, AlA^avaAfiy~u and AlA^avaAfiy , but in both manners in art. vfY ,] M, K;) the latter being allowable; (T,) or, accord. to Akh, the latter only is used by the Arabs; (M;) applied to the three stones mentioned above: (TA in art. sfE ; &c.:) upon these the cooking-pot is set up; but what is of iron, having three legs, is not called Avfy~p , but minoSabN ; (T;) [and this is what is meant by A^avofiy~apN mino HadiydK in art. sfE in the K;] i. e. an iron trivet upon which a cooking-pot is set up. (TA in art. nSb .) A^uvofy~apN may be of the measure fuEoluwyapN [from Avf ], and it may be of the measure A^ufoEuwlapN [from vfY ; in either case originally A^uvofuwyapN ]. (A, L.) vaAlivapu AlA^avaAfiY signifies The part, not detached, of a mountain; by the side of which, two pieces are put [ for the cookingpot to be set thereon ]. (A'Obeyd, T, K.) And hence the saying, (A'Obeyd, T,) ramaAhu All~`hu bvaAlivapi , AlA^avaAfiy (A'Obeyd, T, K) May God smite him with the mountain; meaning, with a calamity; (Th, TA, K in art. vfY ;) with a calamity like the mountain [ in greatness ]; (Th, M;) for when they do not find the third of the AvAfY , they rest the cooking-pot [partly] upon the mountain: (M, K, in art. vfY :) or, with difficulties, or troubles, or calamities: (As, T:) or, with all evil; evils being likened to one Avfy~p after another, and the third being the last: (T, K:) so says Aboo-Sa'eed: (T:) or, with the last of evil; and the last of everything hateful: (AO in Har p. 84:) or, with a great calamity. (Har ib.) One says also, AlA^avaAfiY fulaAnN vaAlivapu , meaning (tropical:) Such a one is the heaviest, most burdensome, or most troublesome, of the people. (Har ubi suprà.) ― -b2- [Hence also,] AlA^avaAfiY is a name applied to (assumed tropical:) certain stars [accord. to Ideler, as mentioned by Freytag in his Lex., the stars σ and τ and υ Draconis ] over against the head of the qidor ; which is the name of certain stars disposed in a round form. (AHát, K.) [Also] a name given by the vulgar to (assumed tropical:) [ The three chief stars in the constellation called ] Al$~aloyaAqu [i. e. Lyra ]. (Kzw.) ― -b3- The sing., (K,) i. e. each of the two forms thereof, but written in the copies of the S with damm [only], (TA in art. vfY ,) or [only] the latter, with kesr, (M, and so in the K in art. vfY ,) also signifies (assumed tropical:) A number, (M,) or a great number, (K, and so in the S in art. vfY ,) and a company, or congregated body, of men: (M, K:) pl. as above. (M.) You say, humo Ealayohi A^uvofiy~apN waAHidapN (assumed tropical:) [ They are against him one band ]. (TA.) And baqiyato mino baniY fulaAnK A^uvofiy~apN xa$onaA='u There remained of the sons of such a one a great number. (S in art. vfY .)

definition: , (S, Msb, K,) originally A^axawN , (Kh, S, Msb,) as is shown by the first of its dual forms mentioned below, and by its having a pl.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) originally A^axawN , (Kh, S, Msb,) as is shown by the first of its dual forms mentioned below, and by its having a pl. like A=baA='K , (S,) and A^ax~N , (K,) with the second letter doubled to compensate for the w suppressed, as is the case in A^ab~N , (TA,) and ↓ A^axFA , [like A^abFA ,] and ↓ A^axuw , (IAar, K, TA, [the last, with the article prefixed to it, erroneously written in the CK AlAuxuw~N ,]) and ↓ A^axowN , like dalowN , (Kr, K,) a well-known term of relationship, (K, TA,) i. e. A brother; the son of one's father and mother, or of either of them: and also applied to a foster-brother: (TA:) and (assumed tropical:) a friend; and a companion, an associate, or a fellow: (K:) derived from A=xiy~apN [q. v.]; as though one A^ax were tied and attached to another like as the horse is tied to the A=xy~p : (Har p. 42 :) or, accord. to some of the grammarians, it is from waxaY meaning qaSada ; because the A^ax has the same aim, endeavour, or desire, as his A^ax : (TA:) when A^ax is prefixed to another noun, its final vowel is prolonged: (Kh:) you say, h*aA A^axuwka [ This is thy brother, &c.], and mararotu biA^axiyka [ I passed by thy brother, &c.], and raA^ayotu A^axaAka [ I saw thy brother, &c.] : (S: [in which it is also asserted that one does not say A^axuw without prefixing it to another noun; but this is inconsistent with the assertion of IAar and F, that AlA^axuw is a syn. of AlA^axu :]) the dual is A^axawaAni , (S, Msb, Kur xlix. 10, Ham p. 434,) or A^axowaAni , with the x quiescent, (TA, [but this I have found nowhere else,]) and some of the Arabs say A^axaAni , (S, Msb,) and Kr mentions A^axuwaAni , with damm to the x , said by IB to occur in poetry, and held by ISd to be dual of A^axuw , with damm to the x : (TA:) the pl. is A_ixowapN and A_ixowaAnN , (S, Msb, K, &c.,) the former generally applied to brothers, and the latter to friends [or the like ], (T, S,*) but not always, as in the Kur xlix. 10, where the former does not denote relationship, and in xxiv. 60 of the same, where the latter does denote relationship, (T, TA,) and sometimes the former is applied to a [single] man, as in the Kur iv. 12, (S,) and A^uxowapN , (Fr, S, Msb, K, [in the CK AaxowapN ,]) or this is a quasi-pl. n., (Sb, TA,) and A^uxowaAnN , (Kr, Msb, K,) and A=xaA='N , (S, K,) like A=baA='N , (S,) and A^uxuw~N , and A^uxuw~apN , (ISd, K,) the last mentioned by Lh, and thought by ISd to be formed from the next preceding by the addition of p characterizing the pl. as fem., (TA,) and A^axuwna , (S, Msb, K,) and AxAwwn . (Msb: [there written without any syll. signs, and I have not found it elsewhere.]) The fem. of A^axN is ↓ A^uxotN [meaning A sister: and (assumed tropical:) a female friend, &c.]: (S, Msb, K, &c. :) written with damm to show that the letter which has gone from it is w ; (S;) the t being a substitute for the w ; (TA;) not to denote the fem. gender, (K, TA,) because the letter next before it is quiescent: this is the opinion of Sb, and [accord. to SM] it is the correct opinion: for Sb says that if you were to use it as a proper name of a man, you would make it perfectly decl.; and if the t were to denote the fem. gender, the name would not be perfectly decl.; though in one place he incidentally says that it is the sign of the fem. gender, through inadvertence: Kh, however, says that its t is [originally] h [meaning p ]: and Lth, that A^uxotN is originally A^axapN : and some say that it is originally A^axowapN : (TA:) the dual. is A^uxotaAni : (Kh:) and the pl. is A^axawaAtN . (Kh, S, Msb, K.) The saying laA A^axaAlaka bifulaAnK [ Thou hast no brother, or (assumed tropical:) friend, in such a one ] means layosa laka biA^axK [ such a one is not a brother, or friend, to thee ]. (S, K.) It is said in a prov., mano laka biA^axiyka kul~ihi [ Who will be responsible to thee for thy brother, or (assumed tropical:) thy friend, altogether? i. e., for his always acting to thee as a brother, or friend]. (JK.) And in another, rub~a A^axK laka lamo talidohu A^um~uka [(assumed tropical:) There is many a brother to thee whom thy mother has not brought forth ]. (TA.) And in another, A^axuwka A^ami Al*~ay^obu [ Is it thy brother, or the wolf? ]; said in suspecting a thing: as also A^axuwka A^ami All~ayolu [ Is it thy brother, or is it the night that deceives thee?]. (Har p. 554.) And another saying is, Alr~umoHu A^axuwka warub~amaA xaAnaka [(assumed tropical:) The spear is thy brother, but sometimes, or often, it is unfaithful to thee ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Ibn-'Arafeh says that when A^uxuw~apN does not relate to birth, it means conformity, or similarity; and combination, agreement, or unison, in action: hence the saying, h*aA Alv~awobu A^axuw h*aA [(assumed tropical:) This garment, or piece of cloth, is the like, or fellow, of this ] : and hence the saying in the Kur [xvii. 29], kaAnuwA A_ixowaAna Al$~ayaATiyni (assumed tropical:) They are the likes, or fellows, of the devils: and in the same [xliii. 47], ↓ A_il~aA hiYa A^akobaru mino A^uxotihaA (assumed tropical:) But it was greater than its like, or fellow; i. e., than what was like to it in truth &c. (TA.) It is said in a trad., Aln~awomu A^axu Almawoti [ Sleep is the like of death ]. (El-Jámi' es-Sagheer.) One says also, laqiYa fulaAnN A^axaA Almawoti (assumed tropical:) Such a one met with the like of death. (Msb, TA.) And they said, lahaA ↓ wamaAhu A=ll~`hu bilayolaPK laA A^uxota [(assumed tropical:) God afflicted him with a night having none like to it ], i. e., a night in which he should die. (TA.) And laA A^ukal~imuhu A_il~aA A^axaA Als~irAri (assumed tropical:) I will not speak to him save the like of secret discourse. (As, TA.) [And hence,] suhayolK ↓ A^uxotaA [(assumed tropical:) The two sisters of Canopus;] the two stars called Al$~EoraY AlEabuwru and Al$~EoraY AlgumayoSaA='u . (S and K in art. $Er , q. v.) ― -b3- yaAa A^axaA bakorK , or tamiymK , means (assumed tropical:) O thou of [the tribe of] Bekr, or Temeem. (Ham p. 284.) ― -b4- Lh mentions, on the authority of Abu-d-Deenár and Ibn-Ziyád, the saying, Alqumomu biA^axiY Al$~ar~a , as meaning (assumed tropical:) The people, or company of men, are in an evil state or condition. (TA.) [But accord. to others,] one says, tarakotuhu biA^axiY Alxayori , meaning (tropical:) I left him in an evil state or condition: (JK, * Msb, K, TA:) and biA^axiY Al$~ar~i (tropical:) in a good state or condition. (TA.) ― -b5- You say also, huwaA^axuw AlS~adoqi (assumed tropical:) He is one who cleaves, or keeps, to veracity. (Msb.) ― -b6- [ A^ixuw , as a prefixed noun, is also used in the sense of A^aholu , meaning (assumed tropical:) Worthy, or deserving, of a thing: and meet, fit, or fitted, for it. So in the phrase A^axuw viqapK (assumed tropical:) Worthy, or deserving, of trust, or confidence; expl. by W (p. 91) as meaning a person in whom one trusts, or confides. And so in the prov., layosa A^axuw AlkiZaAZi mano yasoA^amuhu (assumed tropical:) He who is fit, or fitted, for vehement striving for the mastery is not he who turns away from it with disgust: see art. kZ .] ― -b7- It is also used in the sense of *uw : as in the phrase, huwaA^axuw AlginaY [(assumed tropical:) He is possessed, or a possessor, of wealth, or competence, or sufficiency ]. (Msb.) [So too in the phrase, A^axuw Alxayori (assumed tropical:) Possessed, or a possessor, of good, or of what is good. And in like manner,] A^axuw AlxanaEi means [ *uw AlxanaEi , i. e. *uw Al*~il~api , i. e.] Al~*~aliylu [(assumed tropical:) The low, base, or abject ]. (Ham p. 44.) [So too] sayorunaA A^axuw Aljiyodi means [ sayorunaA *uwAljayodi , i. e.] sayorunaA jaAhidN [(assumed tropical:) Our journeying is laborious: see an ex. in the first paragraph of art. gdr ]. (TA.) ― -b8- Hum~aY AlA^axawayoni (assumed tropical:) A fever that affects the patient two days, and quits him two days; or that attacks on Saturday, and quits for three days, and comes [again] on Thursday; and so on. (Msb.) ― -b9- damu AlA^axawayoni : see damN , in art. dmY .

but this is inconsistent with the assertion of IAar and F, that AlA^axuw is a syn. of AlA^axu :]) the dual is A^axawaAni , (S, Msb, Kur xlix. 10, Ham p. 434,) or A^axowaAni , with the x quiescent, (TA, [but this I have found nowhere else,]) and some of the Arabs say A^axaAni , (S, Msb,) and Kr mentions A^axuwaAni , with damm to the x , said by IB to occur in poetry, and held by ISd to be dual of A^axuw , with damm to the x : (TA:) the pl. is A_ixowapN and A_ixowaAnN , (S, Msb, K, &c.,) the former generally applied to brothers, and the latter to friends [or the like ], (T, S,*) but not always, as in the Kur xlix. 10, where the former does not denote relationship, and in xxiv. 60 of the same, where the latter does denote relationship, (T, TA,) and sometimes the former is applied to a [single] man, as in the Kur iv. 12, (S,) and A^uxowapN , (Fr, S, Msb, K, [in the CK AaxowapN ,]) or this is a quasi-pl. n., (Sb, TA,) and A^uxowaAnN , (Kr, Msb, K,) and A=xaA='N , (S, K,) like A=baA='N , (S,) and A^uxuw~N , and A^uxuw~apN , (ISd, K,) the last mentioned by Lh, and thought by ISd to be formed from the next preceding by the addition of p characterizing the pl. as fem., (TA,) and A^axuwna , (S, Msb, K,) and AxAwwn . (Msb: [there written without any syll. signs, and I have not found it elsewhere.]) The fem. of A^axN is ↓ A^uxotN [meaning A sister: and (assumed tropical:) a female friend, &c.]: (S, Msb, K, &c. :) written with damm to show that the letter which has gone from it is w ; (S;) the t being a substitute for the w ; (TA;) not to denote the fem. gender, (K, TA,) because the letter next before it is quiescent: this is the opinion of Sb, and [accord. to SM] it is the correct opinion: for Sb says that if you were to use it as a proper name of a man, you would make it perfectly decl.; and if the t were to denote the fem. gender, the name would not be perfectly decl.; though in one place he incidentally says that it is the sign of the fem. gender, through inadvertence: Kh, however, says that its t is [originally] h [meaning p ]: and Lth, that A^uxotN is originally A^axapN : and some say that it is originally A^axowapN : (TA:) the dual. is A^uxotaAni : (Kh:) and the pl. is A^axawaAtN . (Kh, S, Msb, K.) The saying laA A^axaAlaka bifulaAnK [ Thou hast no brother, or (assumed tropical:) friend, in such a one ] means layosa laka biA^axK [ such a one is not a brother, or friend, to thee ]. (S, K.) It is said in a prov., mano laka biA^axiyka kul~ihi [ Who will be responsible to thee for thy brother, or (assumed tropical:) thy friend, altogether? i. e., for his always acting to thee as a brother, or friend]. (JK.) And in another, rub~a A^axK laka lamo talidohu A^um~uka [(assumed tropical:) There is many a brother to thee whom thy mother has not brought forth ]. (TA.) And in another, A^axuwka A^ami Al*~ay^obu [ Is it thy brother, or the wolf? ]; said in suspecting a thing: as also A^axuwka A^ami All~ayolu [ Is it thy brother, or is it the night that deceives thee?]. (Har p. 554.) And another saying is, Alr~umoHu A^axuwka warub~amaA xaAnaka [(assumed tropical:) The spear is thy brother, but sometimes, or often, it is unfaithful to thee ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Ibn-'Arafeh says that when A^uxuw~apN does not relate to birth, it means conformity, or similarity; and combination, agreement, or unison, in action: hence the saying, h*aA Alv~awobu A^axuw h*aA [(assumed tropical:) This garment, or piece of cloth, is the like, or fellow, of this ] : and hence the saying in the Kur [xvii. 29], kaAnuwA A_ixowaAna Al$~ayaATiyni (assumed tropical:) They are the likes, or fellows, of the devils: and in the same [xliii. 47], ↓ A_il~aA hiYa A^akobaru mino A^uxotihaA (assumed tropical:) But it was greater than its like, or fellow; i. e., than what was like to it in truth &c. (TA.) It is said in a trad., Aln~awomu A^axu Almawoti [ Sleep is the like of death ]. (El-Jámi' es-Sagheer.) One says also, laqiYa fulaAnN A^axaA Almawoti (assumed tropical:) Such a one met with the like of death. (Msb, TA.) And they said, lahaA ↓ wamaAhu A=ll~`hu bilayolaPK laA A^uxota [(assumed tropical:) God afflicted him with a night having none like to it ], i. e., a night in which he should die. (TA.) And laA A^ukal~imuhu A_il~aA A^axaA Als~irAri (assumed tropical:) I will not speak to him save the like of secret discourse. (As, TA.) [And hence,] suhayolK ↓ A^uxotaA [(assumed tropical:) The two sisters of Canopus;] the two stars called Al$~EoraY AlEabuwru and Al$~EoraY AlgumayoSaA='u . (S and K in art. $Er , q. v.) ― -b3- yaAa A^axaA bakorK , or tamiymK , means (assumed tropical:) O thou of [the tribe of] Bekr, or Temeem. (Ham p. 284.) ― -b4- Lh mentions, on the authority of Abu-d-Deenár and Ibn-Ziyád, the saying, Alqumomu biA^axiY Al$~ar~a , as meaning (assumed tropical:) The people, or company of men, are in an evil state or condition. (TA.) [But accord. to others,] one says, tarakotuhu biA^axiY Alxayori , meaning (tropical:) I left him in an evil state or condition: (JK, * Msb, K, TA:) and biA^axiY Al$~ar~i (tropical:) in a good state or condition. (TA.) ― -b5- You say also, huwaA^axuw AlS~adoqi (assumed tropical:) He is one who cleaves, or keeps, to veracity. (Msb.) ― -b6- [ A^ixuw , as a prefixed noun, is also used in the sense of A^aholu , meaning (assumed tropical:) Worthy, or deserving, of a thing: and meet, fit, or fitted, for it. So in the phrase A^axuw viqapK (assumed tropical:) Worthy, or deserving, of trust, or confidence; expl. by W (p. 91) as meaning a person in whom one trusts, or confides. And so in the prov., layosa A^axuw AlkiZaAZi mano yasoA^amuhu (assumed tropical:) He who is fit, or fitted, for vehement striving for the mastery is not he who turns away from it with disgust: see art. kZ .] ― -b7- It is also used in the sense of *uw : as in the phrase, huwaA^axuw AlginaY [(assumed tropical:) He is possessed, or a possessor, of wealth, or competence, or sufficiency ]. (Msb.) [So too in the phrase, A^axuw Alxayori (assumed tropical:) Possessed, or a possessor, of good, or of what is good. And in like manner,] A^axuw AlxanaEi means [ *uw AlxanaEi , i. e. *uw Al*~il~api , i. e.] Al~*~aliylu [(assumed tropical:) The low, base, or abject ]. (Ham p. 44.) [So too] sayorunaA A^axuw Aljiyodi means [ sayorunaA *uwAljayodi , i. e.] sayorunaA jaAhidN [(assumed tropical:) Our journeying is laborious: see an ex. in the first paragraph of art. gdr ]. (TA.) ― -b8- Hum~aY AlA^axawayoni (assumed tropical:) A fever that affects the patient two days, and quits him two days; or that attacks on Saturday, and quits for three days, and comes [again] on Thursday; and so on. (Msb.) ― -b9- damu AlA^axawayoni : see damN , in art. dmY .

sourceDefinition: , (Lth, S, Msb, K, &c.,) originally of the measure faAEuwlapN , [i. e. A=xuwyapN ,] (Msb,) and A=xiyapN , (Lth, Msb, K,) and A^axiy~apN , (JK, K, TA, [but in the K the orthography of these three words is differently expressed in different copies, and somewhat obscurely in all that I have seen,]) A piece of rope of which the two ends are buried in the ground, (ISk, JK, S,) with a small staff or stick, or a small stone, attached thereto, (ISK, S,) a portion thereof, resembling a loop, being apparent, or exposed, to which the beast is tied; (ISk, JK, S;) it is made in soft ground, as being more commodious to horses than pegs, or stakes, protruding from the ground, and more firm in soft ground than the peg, or stake: (TA:) or a loop tied to a peg, or stake, driven [ into the ground ], to which the beast is attached: (Msb:) or a stick, or piece of wood, (K, TA,) placed crosswise (TA) in a wall, or in a rope of which the two ends are buried in the ground, the [other] end [or portion] protruding, like a ring, to which the beast is tied: (K, TA:) or a peg, or stake, to which horses are tied: (Har p. 42:) [see also A=riY~u :] the pl. of the first is A^awaAxiY~u ; (JK, S, Msb, K;*) and of the second, A^waAxK ; (Msb;) and of the third, A^axaAyaA , (JK, K,*) like as xaTaAyaA is pl. of xaTiy~apN . (TA.) In a trad., the believer and belief are likened to a horse attached to his A=xy~p ; because the horse wheels about, and then returns to his A=xy~p ; and the believer is heedless, and then returns to believe. (TA.) And in another, men are forbidden to make their backs like the A^axaAyaA of beasts; i. e., in prayer; meaning that they should not arch them therein, so as to make them like the loops thus called. (TA.) ― -b2- Also i. q. TunubN ; (K;) i. e. The kind of tent-rope thus called. (TA in art. Tnb , q. v.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) A sacred, or an inviolable, right or the like; syn. HuromapN and *im~apN . (S, K.) You say, lifulaAnK A^awaAxiY~u waA^asobaAbN turoEaY [(assumed tropical:) To such a one belong sacred, or inviolable, rights, and ties of relationship and love, to be regarded ]. (S.) And lahu EinodiY A=jiy~apN (assumed tropical:) He has, with me, or in my estimation, a strong, sacred, or inviolable, right; and a near tie or connexion, or means of access or intimacy or ingratiation. (TA.) ― -b4- In a trad. of 'Omar, in which it is related that he said to El-'Abbás, A^anota A=xiy~apu A=baA='i rasuwli Aall~`hi , it is used in the sense of baqiy~apa ; [and the words may therefore be rendered Thou art the most excellent of the ancestors of the Apostle of God; ] as though he meant, thou art he upon whom one stays himself, and to whom one clings, of the stock of the Apostle of God. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , masc. and fem., and ↓ A_izaArapN , and ↓ miy^ozarN , (S, Msb, K,) and ↓ miy^ozarapN , (Lh,) and ↓ A_izorN , (K,) A thing well known; (S, Msb;) [ a waist-wrapper; ] a wrapper for covering, or which covers, the lower part of the body, [ from the waist downwards, concealing the thighs, and generally the upper half, or more, of the shanks, (see A^azorN , or A^uzorN , and A_izorapN ,)] not sewed: or such as is beneath the shoulders, or on the lower half of the body: the ridaA='i is that which covers the upper half of the body; or that which is upon the shoulders and back; and this also is not sewed: each of these explanations is correct: (MF:) or i. q. miloHafapN : (K:) [in the present day, A_izaAr , vulgarly pronounced A_iyzaAr , is also applied to a woman's outer covering, or wrapper, of white calico; described in my “Modern Egyptians:” and ↓ miy^ozarN , to a pair of drawers: and app., in post-classical writings, to anything resembling a waist-wrapper, worn on any part of the person, and in any manner; sometimes as a turban: ] and A_izaArN also signifies anything with which one is veiled, concealed, or covered: (Th, K:) its pl. is A=zirapN , (S, Msb, K,) a pl. of pauc., (S, Msb,) and (of mult., S, Msb) A^uzurN (S, Msb, K) and A^uzorN , (K,) which is of the dial. of Temeem, or, accord. to MF, a contraction of A^uzurN : (TA:) and the pl. of my^zr is maA=ziru (Msb.) You say, ↓ $ad~a lilA^amori miy^ozarahu (tropical:) He prepared himself for the thing, affair, or business. (A.) And ↓ $ad~a Almiy^ozara (tropical:) He abstained from sexual intercourse: or he prepared himself for religious service. (TA, from a trad.) And AixoDar~a A_izaAriY (tropical:) ( The place of ) my AzAr became black: or, rather, became of a [ blackish ] hue inclining to green: because the hair when it first grows is of that hue. (Har p. 494.) And daAriY A_izaAriY [ My house is my covering ]: said by Es-Sarawee to IAar, on the latter's expressing his surprise at the former's walking in his house naked. (TA.) ― -b2- (tropical:) Continence; chastity. (K, TA.) You say, fulaAnN Eafiyfu AlA_i zaAri , and ↓ Almiy^ozari (tropical:) Such a one is continent, abstaining from women with whom it is unlawful to him to have commerce: (A 'Obeyd:) and in like manner, fulaAnN Tay~bu AlA_izaAri . (TA in art. Hjz .) ― -b3- (tropical:) One's wife: (S, M, K:) or one's self: (IKt, Suh:) or one's wife and family: or one's family and self. (TA.) One says, fidFY laka A_izaAriY (tropical:) May my wife be a ransom for thee: (Aboo-'Omar El-Jarmee, S:) or myself. (IKt, Suh.) And it is said in a trad. respecting the vow of allegiance made at the 'Akabeh, lanamonaEan~aka mim~aA namonaEu minohu A^uzuranaA (tropical:) We will assuredly defend thee from that from which we defend our wives and our families: or ourselves. (TA.) ― -b4- (tropical:) A ewe. (K, TA.) [But see $aApN muw^az~arapN .] And A_izaAro A_izaAro is A cry by which a ewe is called to be milked. (K.)

definition: , used to denote an interrogation, is a compound of the interrogative hemzeh and the negative maA : (M:) it is a mere interrogative [respecting a negative, like A^alaA ];
sourceDefinition: , used to denote an interrogation, is a compound of the interrogative hemzeh and the negative maA : (M:) it is a mere interrogative [respecting a negative, like A^alaA ]; as in the saying, A^amaA tasotaHoyiY mina All~`hi [ Art not thou ashamed for thyself, or of thyself, with respect to God? ]. (Lth, T.) ― -b2- [IHsh says, after explaining two other usages of A^amaA which we have yet to mention,] El-Málakee adds a third meaning of A^amaA , saying that it is a particle denoting EaroDN [or the asking, or requiring, a thing in a gentle manner], like [ A^alaA (q. v.) and] lawolaA ; and is connected peculiarly with a verb; as in A^amaA taquwmu [ Wherefore wilt not thou do stand? ], and A^amaA tafoEalu [ Wherefore wilt not thou do such a thing?]; which may be explained by saying that the hemzeh is used as an interrogative to make one confess, or acknowledge, a thing, as it is in A^alamo and A^alaA , and that maA is a negative. (Mughnee.) ― -b3- It is also an inceptive word, used in the manner of A^alaA : (M:) followed by A^alaA , it is syn. with A^alaA : (S:) [meaning Now: or now surely: or] both of these meaning verily, or truly; i. c. Haq~FA : and for this reason Sb allows one's saying, A^amaA A_n~ah munoTalqN and A^amaA A^an~ahu munoTalqN [ Verily, or truly, he is going away ]; with kesr after the manner of A^alaA A_in~ahu , and with fet-h after the manner of Haq~FA A^an~ahu : and hamaA waAll~`hi laqado kaAna ka*aA is mentioned as meaning A^amaA wa All~`hi [&c., i. e. Verily, or truly, by God, such a thing did indeed happen ]; the h being a substitute for the hemzeh: (M:) so too HamaY wAll~`h [or HamaA wAll~`h ]: (Sgh and K in art. HmY :) it denotes the truth of the words which follow it; as when you say, A^amaA A_in~a zayodFA EaAqilN , meaning Truly, or properly speaking, not tropically, Zeyd is intelligent; and A^am~aA w All~`h qad Daraba zayodN EamorFA [ Truly, &c., by God, Zeyd beat, or struck, Amr ]: (S in art. Amw :) [in other words,] it corroborates an oath and a sentence; as in A^amaA wa All~`h lay^ino soharotu laka layolapF laA^a daEan~aka naAdimFA [ Verily, or now surely, by God, if I remain awake for thee a night, then will I indeed leave thee repenting ]; and A^amaA law Ealimotu makaAnaka laA^azoEajotuka minohu [ Verily, or now surely, if I had known thy place of being, then had I unsettled thee, or removed thee, from it ]; and A^amaA A_in~ahu larajulN kariymN [ Verily, or now surely, he is (emphatically) a generous man ]: (T:) or it is an inceptive particle, used in the manner of A^alaA ; [meaning now: or now surely: ] (Mughnee:) or a particle used to give notice of what is about to be said: only put before a proposition [as in exs. mentioned above]: (TA:) and often occurring before an oath [as in exs. mentioned above]: and sometimes its hemzeh is changed into h or E , before the oath; each with the A remaining; [written hamaA or EamaA ;] and with the A elided; [written hama or Eama ;] or with the A elided, but without the substitution; [written A^ama ;] and when An~a occurs after A^amaA , it is with kesr, as it is after A^alaA : and it also means Haq~FA [ verily, or truly ]: or A^aHq~FA [ verily? or truly? ]: accord. to different opinions: and in this case, An~a after it is with fet-h, as it is after Haq~aA : accord. to Ibn-Kharoof, this is a particle: but some say that it is a noun in the sense of Haq~FA : and others, that it consists of two words, namely, the interrogative hemzeh and maA as a noun in the sense of $aYo'N ; i. e. A^a*Alika Al$~aYo'u Haq~N [ is that thing ture? ]; so that the meaning is A^aHaq~FA : [if so, A^amaA A^an~ah munoTalqN means Verily, or truly, is he going away? ] and this, which is what Sb says, is the correct opinion: maA is virtually in the accus. case, as an adverbial noun, like as Haq~FA is literally: and A^an~a with its complement is an inchoative, of which the adverbial noun is the enunciative: but Mbr says that Haq~FA is the inf. n. of yaHiq~u , which is suppressed, and that A^n~a with its complement is an agent. (Mughnee.)
